record_identity.title: Binance October 2026 wallet-service intrusion through compromised engineer systems and internal AI tooling

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Binance 29 October 2026 wallet-signing compromise and asset theft
incident_identity.date_basis: The Binance 3 November 2026 initial report traces preparations to June and September, a confirmed internal-AI-tool pivot on 20 October, and the main wallet-signing attack on 29–30 October UTC. The exact day of June and September preparatory activity is unavailable; 1 June marks only a bounded earliest month and does not assert an actual event on that day.

summary: In June and September 2026, attackers gained access to computers used by Binance engineers. One engineer had earlier downloaded a tampered installer while seeking an AI coding tool. Another was approached through a fake recruitment process and persuaded to run a malicious programming assignment on a work computer. On 20 October, the attackers used the compromised computer and Binance's internal AI tool to reach two more engineers' computers and found a credential permitting container deployments. On 29 October, they used stolen credentials and a malicious container to enter Binance's wallet-signing systems and transfer digital assets to attacker-controlled wallets. They also used Ethereum's EIP-7702 delegation feature, enabling further transfers after normal withdrawals were suspended. Binance reported approximately US$6.34 billion in affected assets, with about US$2.85 billion frozen or intercepted by 3 November. It said customers would be compensated. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation, which North Korea denies. Binance has not identified the AI tool's exact permissions or shown whether an AI agent independently selected any of the attack actions.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Binance's 3 November initial forensic report attributes an initial June compromised installer and a September fake-interview malware download to attacker preparation. The report says Engineer B's compromised device was used with an internal AI tool to gain control of Engineers A and C on 20 October; it does not disclose the AI runtime, prompts, agent execution logs, privileges or the individual sequence of tool actions. Binance reports attacker access to a container deployment token on Engineer A's computer, later login to Engineer C's computer, use of A's stolen credentials and deployment of a malicious container on 29 October. A malicious script gained access to an internal signing service and enabled unauthorised transfers of XRP, SOL, OP, BTC and ETH. The attacker used EIP-7702 delegation transactions on an Ethereum hot wallet, meaning ordinary withdrawal suspension did not revoke on-chain execution authority. Binance reports the last unauthorised transfer finalised 29 October at 23:56 UTC and that it cleared delegation at 00:10 UTC on 30 October. Binance reported US$6.34 billion in affected digital assets, US$2.85 billion frozen or intercepted as at 3 November, and replenishment of 98% of impacted token assets in its reserves by 31 October. Its report says the investigation remains open. The FBI formally attributes the theft to TraderTraitor actors linked to North Korea and describes laundering observations, while North Korea disputes the attribution. Reuters provides independent reporting of the disclosure, not independent access to all forensic records.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The established occurrence is an attacker-controlled cyber intrusion using malicious software, social engineering and an internal AI tool as a cross-workstation access pathway, followed by unauthorised wallet-signing activity. The source establishes that the AI tool was materially used but not whether the tool autonomously selected workstations, escalated privileges or violated its own intended task authority. Nor does it establish that the tool had unrestricted company-wide access: the two engineers reached and the stolen deployment token provide a narrower observed path. Thus the observed attacker-directed compromise cannot be converted into an AI Fidelity Class result without actor-action and permission evidence. The defensive detection of the June compromise, the October alert, withdrawal suspension, freezing efforts and wallet revocation are preserved as contextual outcomes and controls of Binance and its partners, not as successful invariants attributed to the attacking AI system. The large financial consequence is assessed separately from uncertain AI-specific classification.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: This case shows how human-targeted deception and software supply-chain compromise can combine with an internal AI service, shared access to engineering workstations, stolen deployment credentials and smart-contract delegation to produce large real-world consequences. It is a strong test of actor-action attribution, effective versus intended tool authority, custody of authentication materials, and the difference between model behaviour, attacker misuse and downstream cryptocurrency authorisation controls.
assessment_boundaries: Binance's 3 November publication is an initial report; an independent forensic review and some technical disclosure are pending.
The internal AI tool is unnamed. No agent topology, detailed session logs, prompts, policy limits or per-action autonomous decisions have been published.
Observed reach to Engineers A and C is not proof of unrestricted company-wide permissions or absence of all access controls.
Employee compromise and malicious scripts are established by the provider's report; a distinct autonomous AI decision or misalignment mechanism is not.
The FBI's attribution to TraderTraitor is an external investigator's finding, not independently reconstructed by VIGIL; North Korea denies responsibility.

The amount of US$6.34 billion describes reported affected/transferred assets. US$2.85 billion was frozen or intercepted by 3 November; later recovery, final net loss and token valuation remain subject to reconciliation.
Binance's replenishment of reserves and undertaking to absorb customer losses do not erase the occurrence's unauthorised movement of funds and do not establish the final cost.
Binance's reported 57 thwarted suspected North Korea-linked attempts during 2026 are background and are not separate incidents collapsed into this occurrence.
No public evidence establishes how much of the theft was caused by an AI tool independently rather than human-authored malware, stolen credentials and on-chain execution.
Defender controls and remedial actions are not adjudicated as positive mappings to the attacker/originating system.

source_clause_analysis.purpose: Chronological source-first propositions preserving attacker-directed use of an internal AI tool, narrower attribution limits, externally governed wallet access, on-chain authorisations and distinct defender outcomes.

clauses.source_paraphrase: In June, Engineer A downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while seeking an AI coding tool; Binance detected an anomaly, replaced the device and rotated related credentials, but role/team information had been exposed.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A supply-chain compromise and bounded detection are reported. Exposure of team roles persisted after endpoint remediation, but the installer is not evidence of autonomous AI behaviour.

clauses.source_paraphrase: In September, a purported recruiter and CEO of a fictitious company conducted a staged interview of Engineer B, eventually requesting a programming assignment that was downloaded onto a company device.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: The human-directed deception created a credible intrusion route; the social-engineering campaign cannot by itself be called an AI-agent failure.

clauses.source_paraphrase: The malicious assignment replaced a development-tool component with obfuscated malware able to contact an attacker server and evade then-current endpoint detection.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: The compromise mechanism was executable malware operating after a deceptive download. The source does not assign these steps to an autonomous model.

clauses.source_paraphrase: On 20 October, attackers used Engineer B's compromised computer and an internal Binance AI tool to gain control over the computers of Engineers A and C.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: An internal AI tool materially participated in the access pathway. The exact action attribution, permission model, tool commands and autonomous choices are not public.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: The statement distinguishes an attacker-operated workstation from the internal AI tool but does not identify which actions were model-selected, attacker-directed or merely executed under an existing session. Actor-action attribution cannot be resolved from a vendor summary.

clauses.adjudication_note: The current evidence does not resolve an AI-system action and its intended governance boundary; additional internal tool logs or independent forensic evidence are needed.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Following the 20 October pivot, the attacker found a token on Engineer A's computer permitting container deployment.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: The attacker's access to protected authentication material is reported; the evidence does not show whether AI execution discovered or transferred the token.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: A container deployment token was found on a compromised workstation. The published record does not tie its retrieval or custody transfer to an identified AI action rather than the human operator or malware.

clauses.adjudication_note: The current evidence does not resolve an AI-system action and its intended governance boundary; additional internal tool logs or independent forensic evidence are needed.

clauses.source_paraphrase: On 29 October from 17:15–19:56 UTC, the attackers logged into Engineer C's computer, used credentials stolen from Engineer A and deployed a container and malicious script against wallet signing.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: The execution path demonstrates credential misuse and unauthorised infrastructure access but does not document the AI tool's continued role after 20 October.

clauses.source_paraphrase: On 29 October from 20:05–20:09 UTC, five hot wallets transferred 233.46 million XRP to the attacker; other Binance hot wallets sent SOL, OP and BTC in unauthorised transfers.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Unauthorised asset movements were realised, with substantial financial consequences; the amount is not a finding of autonomous AI choice.

clauses.source_paraphrase: The attacker used the compromised signing service to establish malicious EIP-7702 smart-contract delegation on an Ethereum hot wallet, using multiple signing transactions including nonce manipulation.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: On-chain delegation extended attacker-controlled execution beyond the normal Binance withdrawal infrastructure; the mechanism is blockchain authorisation misuse, not evidenced agent permission delegation.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Binance detected large-volume transfers, suspended normal withdrawals and coordinated freezing. Existing malicious on-chain delegation remained operative, requiring additional revocation steps.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A defender's containment steps worked partially and in stages; they did not immediately invalidate independent on-chain authorisations. They are not classified as successful invariants of the attacking AI.

clauses.source_paraphrase: The final unauthorised transaction of 2,961.9 ETH finalised at 23:56 UTC on 29 October; Binance removed the EIP-7702 delegated code via an authorisation to the zero address at 00:10 UTC on 30 October.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: The defender completed a distinct on-chain revocation after the last known unauthorised transfer. No AI-driven safe termination behaviour is established.

clauses.source_paraphrase: The FBI's 31 October cyber alert attributed the 29 October Binance theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation and published associated laundering addresses; North Korea later denied responsibility.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: This is third-party attacker attribution and downstream laundering evidence. It does not demonstrate which internal AI actions occurred.

clauses.source_paraphrase: On 3 November Binance disclosed about US$6.34 billion in affected assets and US$2.85 billion frozen or intercepted, said 98% of impacted token reserves had been replenished by 31 October, and committed to cover user losses.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Large materialised unauthorised transfers, partial freezing and provider restitution are separate facts. Restitution is not a reason to downgrade original transfer severity or assert net loss without reconciliation.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Binance reported rebuilding the affected internal AI tool and its access controls, replacing impacted devices, invalidating credentials, strengthening anomaly detection and commissioning independent review.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Remediation confirms the AI tooling was sufficiently implicated for rebuilding, but does not identify the former permissions or establish autonomous policy violations.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: The tool's access controls were rebuilt following the intrusion, but no published specification of intended permissions or recorded AI action establishes a failure or holding of its own authority boundary.

clauses.adjudication_note: The current evidence does not resolve an AI-system action and its intended governance boundary; additional internal tool logs or independent forensic evidence are needed.

agent_context.evidence_basis: Binance states an internal AI tool was used to reach two additional engineer endpoints, but does not establish that it was an autonomous agent, its topology or how its commands were selected.

occurrence_environment.environment_detail: An internally deployed AI-enabled engineering tool was operated during a real, unauthorised production-network intrusion. Tool architecture and degree of agency remain unspecified.
occurrence_environment.evidence_basis: A real internal AI tool participated in a production attack path. Its exact model and agentic capabilities are unresolved; the operational tool was live rather than a contained test.

entities.name: Binance hot-wallet signing service
entities.evidence_basis: Unauthorised signing-service access and smart-contract delegation initiated transfers outside the normal withdrawal process.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The attacker made material use of a Binance internal AI tool to access two additional employees' machines, but the provider did not release the agent's execution trace or its permitted and actual task scope. Independent AI selection, actor-control transfers and relevant FC recognition conditions are unresolved. The malicious installer, recruitment deception, stolen credentials and blockchain authorisation use establish an external cyberattack, not automatically an AI-system misalignment. No canonical mapping is asserted until an identifiable model or agent action is supported; candidate relationships remain non-canonical.

The attacker obtained real non-public authentication material (a deployment token and engineer credentials) through compromised workstations; exact sensitivity and any separate personal-data disclosure remain unknown. Confirmed unauthorised access to confidential authentication materials establishes the S2 minimum, not a population-wide data breach.

Binance reported real unauthorised transfers involving an estimated US$6.34 billion in digital assets; the FBI independently described more than US$6 billion stolen. As of 3 November Binance reported US$2.85 billion frozen or intercepted. Realised illicit outflows demonstrably exceed the S4 threshold of US$100 million, but the gross transferred amount must not be treated as final unrecovered net loss, and the costs to customers versus the exchange remain distinct.
